theme: Israel’s history of unfaithfulness, grace despite rebellion
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 106:1-23. This is a confession psalm, a summary of Israel’s early failures told from the standpoint of people who know that their own record is no better. Read it slowly and listen for the one line that keeps the history from being a list of defeats.
settingTheScene: You have just begun the story of the exodus, and this psalm looks back on it from centuries later. It is one of the great historical psalms of the Bible, along with Psalms 78, 105, and 136. The author does not know the details of how it will all turn out, but he knows that Israel has a long history of failing God, and that God has a long history of being faithful. The psalm will return in two parts, and between them you will read the whole exodus story. Think of it as a preview.
observation: The psalm begins with praise: “Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever!” (v. 1).
A confession follows: “Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness” (v. 6).
At the Red Sea, the fathers “did not consider your wondrous works…but rebelled by the sea” (v. 7).
“Yet he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his mighty power” (v. 8).
“He rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry” (v. 9). “Then they believed his words; they sang his praise” (v. 12).
“But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel” (v. 13).
In the wilderness, they “craved to the full,” and God “gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them” (vv. 14-15).
The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram, who challenged Moses’ authority (vv. 16-18).
“They made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a metal image. They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (vv. 19-20).
“Therefore he said he would destroy them, had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them” (v. 23).
interpretation:
The structure of the psalm is a lesson in itself. It begins and ends with praise. In the middle, it tells a long story of failure. The psalm is not a bitter complaint about Israel. It is an act of worship that tells the truth about sin and the truth about God.

Notice the first confession in verse 6: “Both we and our fathers have sinned.” The psalmist does not blame his ancestors. He includes himself. This is the heart of honest confession. It is not enough to say that the past generation failed. We are part of the same story, with the same tendencies.

Then look at the pattern in the history. Israel sees a miracle and believes. A few days later, they forget. This is the thing the psalm keeps saying: “They soon forgot his works.” Forgetting is a form of sin, and it is the root of other sins. When you stop remembering what God has done, you stop trusting what he will do. This is why the Bible so often calls people to remember: to keep the Passover, to set up memorial stones, to tell the story to children.

The most shocking detail is verse 20: “They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass.” It is meant to sound absurd. The people have seen the greatest display of God’s power in history, and they traded it for a statue of a grass-eating animal. Paul will pick up this phrase in Romans 1:23 to describe the human condition. We all do this, with money, success, comfort, and image.

But the line that carries the psalm is verse 8. “Yet he saved them for his name’s sake.” God’s rescue does not depend on Israel’s merit, since they did not have any. It rests on his own character and name. That is the foundation of grace.

The last verse in the section points to a mediator. “Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach.” A breach is a gap in a wall, and a man standing in it takes the full force of the attack. God would have destroyed Israel, but Moses stepped between. It is a picture of what Christ will do on a much grander scale.
connection: Paul uses the phrase of verse 20 in Romans 1:23, and in 1 Corinthians 10:1-13 he uses Israel’s wilderness history as a warning and encouragement to the church. Hebrews 3:7-19 calls believers not to harden their hearts as Israel did. Ezekiel 22:30 describes God looking for someone to “stand in the breach” and finding no one. Jesus stands in that breach fully.
application:
Make a short list of what God has done for you in the past year. Put it somewhere you will see it. Forgetting is the first step toward drifting.

Confess honestly, as the psalmist does, using the word “we.” Pray for your church and community, not only for yourself.

Ask yourself what you are tempted to exchange for the glory of God, and bring it to Christ.
prayerPrompts: Confess the lesser things you have exchanged for God’s glory.
Thank him for saving you for his name’s sake.
Thank him for the one who stands in the breach for you.
